mathleague-2012-13-g6-01.title: Count up
mathleague-2012-13-g6-01.body:
From 21 to 28 is 7 steps, so 7 flights were in the daytime.

**Answer: (A) 7**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-02.title: Group two of the numbers
mathleague-2012-13-g6-02.body:
$12 + 34 = 46$, so the sum is $46 + 56$ (A). $34 + 56 = 90$ gives (B), and $12 + 56 = 68$ gives (C). (D) uses 46 and 68, which double-counts the 12.

**Answer: (D) $46+68$**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-04.title: Subtract one at a time
mathleague-2012-13-g6-04.body:
Taking away $43 + 21$ is the same as taking away 43 and then taking away 21. So the blank is 21.

**Answer: (C) 21**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-04.title: Compute
mathleague-2012-13-g6-04.body:
Left side: $65 - 64 = 1$. Right side: $65 - 43 = 22$, and $22 - 21 = 1$. So the blank is 21.

**Answer: (C) 21**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-05.title: Subtract
mathleague-2012-13-g6-05.body:
One dime less than \$1 is 90¢. The dime and quarter are worth 35¢. The pocket holds $90 - 35 = 55$¢.

**Answer: (B) 55¢**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-06.title: Count back
mathleague-2012-13-g6-06.body:
Five days before Wednesday: Tuesday, Monday, Sunday, Saturday, Friday.

**Answer: (A) Friday**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-06.title: Count forward from the answer
mathleague-2012-13-g6-06.body:
From Friday: Saturday (1), Sunday (2), Monday (3), Tuesday (4), Wednesday (5) ✓.

**Answer: (A) Friday**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-07.title: One prime must be 2
mathleague-2012-13-g6-07.body:
Each choice is odd. Two odd primes add to an even number, so one of the primes must be 2. Then the other is the choice minus 2: $9, 15, 21, 29$. Only 29 is prime, so $31 = 2 + 29$.

**Answer: (D) 31**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-08.title: Pairs
mathleague-2012-13-g6-08.body:
12 shoes is 6 pairs, and each pair weighs 12 kg: $6 \times 12 = 72$ kg.

**Answer: (D) 72 kg**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-08.title: One shoe
mathleague-2012-13-g6-08.body:
One shoe weighs $12 \div 2 = 6$ kg, so 12 shoes weigh $12 \times 6 = 72$ kg.

**Answer: (D) 72 kg**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-10.title: Count the items
mathleague-2012-13-g6-10.body:
Six dozen = 72. One dozen pairs = $12 \times 2 = 24$. Total $72 + 24 = 96$, and $96 \div 3 = 32$ sets of three.

**Answer: (B) 32**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-10.title: Dozens
mathleague-2012-13-g6-10.body:
One dozen pairs is 2 dozen, so the total is 8 dozen. Each dozen makes 4 sets of three, so 8 dozen make $8 \times 4 = 32$.

**Answer: (B) 32**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-11.title: Remainder 3
mathleague-2012-13-g6-11.body:
We need a number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4. $31 = 4 \times 7 + 3$ ✓.

**Answer: (A) 31**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-11.title: Check the others
mathleague-2012-13-g6-11.body:
32 is a multiple of 4 (remainder 0), 33 leaves 1, and 34 leaves 2. Only 31 leaves 3.

**Answer: (A) 31**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-12.title: Change to hours
mathleague-2012-13-g6-12.body:
$420 \div 60 = 7$ hours. Seven hours before 4 P.M. is 9 A.M.

**Answer: (C) 9:00 A.M.**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-12.title: Count forward
mathleague-2012-13-g6-12.body:
From 9 A.M. to noon is 3 hours, and noon to 4 P.M. is 4 hours: 7 hours = 420 minutes ✓.

**Answer: (C) 9:00 A.M.**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-13.title: Regroup
mathleague-2012-13-g6-13.body:
10 hundreds is 1 thousand, 10 tens is 1 hundred, 10 ones is 1 ten: 1 thousand + 1 hundred + 1 ten = 1110.

**Answer: (C) 1110**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-14.title: Try the choices
mathleague-2012-13-g6-14.body:
Subtract 7 from each choice to get last year, then add: $(25 - 7) + 25 = 18 + 25 = 43$ ✓.

**Answer: (B) 25**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-14.title: Remove the extra
mathleague-2012-13-g6-14.body:
Take the extra 7 away: $43 - 7 = 36$ is twice last year's number, so last year was 18 and this year is $18 + 7 = 25$.

**Answer: (B) 25**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-15.title: Groups
mathleague-2012-13-g6-15.body:
3 trapezoids have 12 sides, the same as 4 triangles. 27 trapezoids is 9 such groups, matching $9 \times 4 = 36$ triangles.

**Answer: (D) 36**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-16.title: Groups of 11
mathleague-2012-13-g6-16.body:
Each group has 6 roses and 5 daisies, 11 flowers. $66 \div 11 = 6$ groups, so $6 \times 6 = 36$ roses.

**Answer: (D) 36**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-17.title: Even/odd rules
mathleague-2012-13-g6-17.body:
odd + odd = even, and even + even = even. So the sum must be even. Only 52 is even.

**Answer: (A) 52**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-17.title: Example
mathleague-2012-13-g6-17.body:
$1 + 3 + 48 = 52$ uses two different odd numbers and an even number.

**Answer: (A) 52**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-18.title: Make a table
mathleague-2012-13-g6-18.body:
Sun 2, Mon 4, Tue 8, Wed 16, Thu 32, Fri 64, Sat 128. The first day with more than 100 is Saturday.

**Answer: (C) Saturday**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-18.title: Powers of 2
mathleague-2012-13-g6-18.body:
After $n$ days there are $2 \times 2^n$ rabbits. $2 \times 2^5 = 64 < 100$ but $2 \times 2^6 = 128 > 100$, so 6 days after Sunday: Saturday.

**Answer: (C) Saturday**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-19.title: Think in pawpaws
mathleague-2012-13-g6-19.body:
A pomegranate costs the same as 4 pawpaws. It costs 50¢ more than 2 pawpaws, so the other 2 pawpaws cost 50¢. Then 4 pawpaws, which equal one pomegranate, cost \$1.

**Answer: (C) \$1**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-19.title: Try the choices
mathleague-2012-13-g6-19.body:
If the pomegranate costs \$1, a pawpaw costs 25¢, 2 pawpaws cost 50¢, and \$1 is 50¢ more ✓.

**Answer: (C) \$1**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-20.title: Simplify the steps
mathleague-2012-13-g6-20.body:
Tripling then dividing by 6 is the same as halving. Half of the number is 18, so the number is 36.

**Answer: (B) 36**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-22.title: Test the choices
mathleague-2012-13-g6-22.body:
If Bob has jumped 12 times: after 15 more he has 27. Three jumps ago he had 9, and $3 \times 9 = 27$ ✓.

**Answer: (A) 12**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-22.title: Use algebra
mathleague-2012-13-g6-22.body:
Let $n$ be the jumps so far. $n + 15 = 3(n - 3) = 3n - 9$, so $2n = 24$ and $n = 12$.

**Answer: (A) 12**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-23.title: Compare values
mathleague-2012-13-g6-23.body:
10 nickels = 50¢ and 9 dimes = 90¢, total 140¢. 5 quarters = 125¢. $140 - 125 = 15$ pennies.

**Answer: (D) 15**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-24.title: Ones digit 5
mathleague-2012-13-g6-24.body:
5 times an odd number always ends in 5: 5, 15, 25, ..., 95. That is 10 numbers.

**Answer: (B) 10**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-24.title: Count the odd numbers
mathleague-2012-13-g6-24.body:
We need $5 \times k < 100$ with $k$ odd, so $k$ is an odd number less than 20: 1, 3, ..., 19. There are 10 of them.

**Answer: (B) 10**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-25.title: Divisibility shortcuts
mathleague-2012-13-g6-25.body:
For 4, look at the last two digits: $23 = 20 + 3$, remainder 3. For 5, look at the last digit: 4 is 4 more than 0, remainder 4. 345 is odd, remainder 1 when divided by 2. Sum 8.

**Answer: (C) 8**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-27.title: Count the magnets
mathleague-2012-13-g6-27.body:
Last month: \$24 ÷ \$0.80 = 30 magnets. This month: \$24 ÷ \$1.20 = 20 magnets. 50 magnets cost \$48, so the average is \$48 ÷ 50 = \$0.96.

**Answer: (B) \$0.96**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-27.title: Not \$1.00!
mathleague-2012-13-g6-27.body:
The plain average of 80¢ and \$1.20 is \$1.00, but I bought more of the cheaper magnets, so the average must be less than \$1.00. Ruling out (C) and (D), the exact count above gives \$0.96.

**Answer: (B) \$0.96**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-28.title: Midpoint
mathleague-2012-13-g6-28.body:
The point halfway between is their average: $(1.75 + 7.25) \div 2 = 9 \div 2 = 4.5$.

**Answer: (D) 4.5**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-29.title: Count factors of 2 and 3
mathleague-2012-13-g6-29.body:
Count how many 2s appear: $2^3$ gives 3, $4^5$ gives $2 \times 5 = 10$, $6^7$ gives 7 — total 20. Count 3s: $3^4$ gives 4, $6^7$ gives 7, $9^{10}$ gives $2 \times 10 = 20$ — total 31.

**Answer: (B) $2^{20} \times 3^{31}$**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-30.title: Match the black cars
mathleague-2012-13-g6-30.body:
Black cars appear as 5 in one ratio and 3 in the other, so use 15 black cars: red:black = 8:5 = 24:15 and black:white = 3:4 = 15:20. The smallest total is $24 + 15 + 20 = 59$.

**Answer: (B) 59**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-30.title: Why it's the minimum
mathleague-2012-13-g6-30.body:
The number of black cars must be a multiple of both 5 and 3, so at least 15. With 15 black cars there are 24 red and 20 white; any larger multiple of 15 makes all counts bigger. Minimum 59.

**Answer: (B) 59**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-31.title: Find the middle
mathleague-2012-13-g6-31.body:
$25 + 26 + 27 + 28 + 29 + 30 = 165$. Ten consecutive integers with sum 165 have average $165 \div 10 = 16.5$, so the middle two are 16 and 17. The numbers are 12 to 21, and the largest is 21.

**Answer: (C) 21**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-31.title: Check 12 to 21
mathleague-2012-13-g6-31.body:
Pair them: $12 + 21 = 13 + 20 = \ldots = 16 + 17 = 33$, five pairs, $5 \times 33 = 165$ ✓. And $25 + \ldots + 30$ is three pairs of 55, also 165.

**Answer: (C) 21**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-32.title: Find radius, width, length
mathleague-2012-13-g6-32.body:
Area $\pi r^2 = 36\pi$ means $r^2 = 36$, so $r = 6$ cm. Width = 6 cm. Diameter = 12 cm, which is half the length, so length = 24 cm. Perimeter $= 2 \times (6 + 24) = 60$ cm.

**Answer: (A) 60 cm**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-32.title: In radii
mathleague-2012-13-g6-32.body:
Width = 1 radius, length = 2 diameters = 4 radii. Perimeter = $2 \times (1 + 4) = 10$ radii $= 10 \times 6 = 60$ cm.

**Answer: (A) 60 cm**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-33.title: Blocks of four
mathleague-2012-13-g6-33.body:
In every block of 4 numbers (1–4, 5–8, ...), 3 numbers are kept. $2345 = 3 \times 781 + 2$. So 781 full blocks (up to $4 \times 781 = 3124$) give 2343 kept numbers, and two more kept numbers are 3125 and 3126. The largest is 3126.

**Answer: (A) 3126**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-33.title: Check the choices
mathleague-2012-13-g6-33.body:
Up to 3126 there are $3126 \div 4 = 781$ R 2, so 781 multiples of 4. Kept: $3126 - 781 = 2345$ ✓. Also, the largest number left can't be a multiple of 4, and 3127 would give 2346.

**Answer: (A) 3126**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-34.title: Falling behind
mathleague-2012-13-g6-34.body:
On schedule, the last 6 days would need $6 \times 120 = 720$ boxes, but 1200 remain — I am $1200 - 720 = 480$ boxes behind. Each 90-box day put me 30 boxes behind, so there were $480 \div 30 = 16$ such days. In all: $16 + 6 = 22$ days.

**Answer: (C) 22**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-34.title: Check 22 days
mathleague-2012-13-g6-34.body:
The job is $22 \times 120 = 2640$ boxes. In 16 days at 90 a day I load 1440, leaving $2640 - 1440 = 1200$ for the last 6 days ✓.

**Answer: (C) 22**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-35.title: Work backwards
mathleague-2012-13-g6-35.body:
Each day's count is $\frac{3}{2}$ of the day before, so each earlier day is $\frac{2}{3}$ of the next. Fri 2430, Thu 1620, Wed 1080, Tue 720, Mon 480, Sun 320.

**Answer: (D) 320**

mathleague-2012-13-g6-35.title: Forward check
mathleague-2012-13-g6-35.body:
Start with 320 on Sunday and multiply by 1.5 five times: 480, 720, 1080, 1620, 2430 ✓.

**Answer: (D) 320**
